title: IEA Oil Market Report (October 2026)
source: EST: re-derived this session, not read at a primary. `iea.org` returned HTTP 403 on every path tried today — `/events/oil-market-report-october-2026`, `/data-and-statistics/data-product/oil-market-report-omr`, and the bare domain — to both a browser-UA `curl` and a converting fetcher (the latter returning only "Enable JavaScript and cookies to continue"), the FOURTH consecutive research session this event has met that wall (2026-09-06, 2026-09-15 x2, 2026-09-29). investing.com's IEA Monthly Oil Market Report calendar page (economic-calendar/iea-monthly-report-1674) was re-fetched today and is now MORE stale than when the proposal cited it: it still lists "Sep 11, 2026 09:00" as the NEXT release, eighteen days after that edition actually published — the aggregator's forward pointer has not moved in over two weeks and cannot be used for this date. What corroborates the date instead: a search index returned the IEA's own event page at `iea.org/events/oil-market-report-october-2026` — a URL the Agency itself created and titled for this specific edition, existing before the report ships, the same naming convention its already-published `oil-market-report-{month}-2026` event pages use (august, april, march editions all confirmed reachable the same way) — plus independent search-engine snippets naming 14 October 2026 as the release and 13 November 2026 as the one after it. Neither is a primary date string read off a rendered page (the 403 wall blocks that), so this is corroboration by the page's existence and by a second index's snippet, not a read. The standing IEA cadence this calendar has tracked since 2025-12-11 (11DEC2025, 21JAN2026, 12MAR2026 [no Feb 2026 edition found published], 14APR2026, 13MAY2026, 17JUN2026, 10JUL2026, 12AUG2026, 11SEP2026) runs irregularly inside a 10th-to-21st-of-the-month band with no fixed weekday rule; 2026-10-14 sits inside that band. STAYS ESTIMATE on the same four counts the proposal gave, none resolved this session: the primary schedule page is still unreadable, the aggregator table is stale in a new way (frozen on an edition that already published), the source-prefix taxonomy in `market-events-data.ts` defines no `IEA:` confirmed prefix, and this lane may not self-confirm an event it discovered in-sweep (here, promoted from a sibling's proposal). Release time carried forward at the IEA's standing 10:00 Paris = 04:00 ET — Paris is still CEST and the US is still EDT on 2026-10-14, so the UTC offset that gave `iea-omr-2026-09-11` its 04:00 ET reading is unchanged. Re-derived 2026-09-29
notes: Promoted from the single sibling proposal `proposals/iea-omr-2026-10-14.from-iea-omr-2026-09-11.json`, filed by the `iea-omr-2026-09-11` close-out on 2026-09-15 (that ledger's own October OMR date was never verified and is not itself a source this file relies on beyond corroborating the cadence). Two live questions this edition inherits, both read in full from the September close-out. (1) THE IEA-MINUS-EIA GULF SHUT-IN OFFSET, stated there as a hypothesis with no owner because a test scoring in October would have orphaned on a closed ledger: the two agencies' same-month Gulf/Mideast shut-in figures differ by a near-constant ~3.35 mb/d (July: 8.3 IEA vs 4.98 EIA = 3.32; August: 10.1 IEA vs 6.72 EIA = 3.38) — a definitional gap between two different baselines (IEA implied pre-war 32.0 mb/d vs EIA's Feb-26 25.2 mb/d, 6.8 apart), not a live disagreement. This edition is the September-month test: EIA's October STEO (`eia-steo-2026-10-06`, publishes eight days earlier) and this OMR both report September, so both readings exist before this event's own close-out window closes. Registered as FT-iea-omr-2026-10-14-2 in this PR. (2) THE RELEASE-WINDOW BASE RATE, now n=14 with the real 2026-09-11 observation folded in (the September close-out's own re-score, not re-measured here): the p90 threshold broke on both crude benchmarks that day, but the OMR was not identifiable as the cause — three of the day's outlier hours closed before the report existed, and the close-out named the actual test design flaw: a threshold plus a prose attribution clause is unscoreable exactly when the tape is interesting enough to be worth testing. This edition's forward test (FT-iea-omr-2026-10-14-1) pre-registers the fix — the same session's other 20 hourly bars scored against their own-hour 2-year distribution, plus NG=F as a placebo — so attribution is measured at registration, not argued after the fact. THE REGIME HAS NOT COOLED SINCE THE LAST EDITION, which is why this event is read as higher-stakes than its `low` impact tier alone suggests: the Saudi East-West pipeline (the main bypass route around the Strait, ~4-5 mb/d) was struck 2026-09-10, shut as a precaution, restarted 2026-09-22 at a "low rate" with "full resumption tak[ing] weeks" (Bloomberg/Hydrocarbon Processing, 2026-09-22 — cross-cited from `opec-plus-meeting-2026-10-04`'s 2026-09-27 pulse, not re-verified here), and Brent round-tripped from a post-attack 108.75 (09-15) to 97.44 (09-25, giving back the entire spike) to a reported ~$105-108 (09-26 to 09-28, on Trump rejecting an Iranian Hormuz-reopening proposal) inside three weeks — the OMR's own September-data read of the bypass route and Gulf exports is the first agency-grade number on a month that was this volatile start to finish. Filed `low` on the same reasoning as its September sibling and every other forecast-publication entry on this calendar: it sets no policy and moves no equity tape, and `symbols: []` follows the calendar's own convention for macro/geopolitical entries.
